title: Remark
body_md:
As $k_1,k_2 \to \infty$, Theorem \ref{thm_upperbound} recovers our previous result \cite{DongYangZhu26}*{Theorem 1.4}. In particular, estimates \eqref{grad_u_upperbound3} and \eqref{grad_u_lower_bound_new} reveal a new blow-up phenomenon at the critical bonding parameter, caused by the resonance between two inclusions of finite conductivity.
		Moreover, the constant $C$ in \eqref{grad_u_upperbound1} depends on $\gamma$ through $\gamma_0$ and the positive lower bound of $1- \gamma\mu$, while the constant in \eqref{grad_u_upperbound2} depends on $\gamma$ only through the positive lower bound of $\gamma\mu - 1$ { but does not depend on the upper bound of $\gamma$}. As a consequence, estimate \eqref{grad_u_upperbound2} { is consistent with} the optimal gradient estimate for the insulated problem obtained in \cite{DLY} as $\gamma \to \infty$. We note that the discussion on $\gamma$ dependence does not apply to Theorems \ref{thm_upperbound_3} and \ref{thm_upperbound_2} below.

label: v_upper
title: Proof
body_md:
By considering $u_\pm -\sup_{\partial \Omega} \varphi$ in place of $u_\pm$, we may assume $u_+\le 0$ on $\partial\Omega$, and it suffices to show that
		\begin{equation}\label{v_upper}
			u \le 0 \quad \mbox{in } \Omega.
		\end{equation}
		We denote $v_1:=\max\{u_+,0\}$ and $v_2:=\max\{u_-,0\}$. We multiply the first equation in \eqref{subrobin} by $v_1$ and integrate by parts in $\widetilde\Omega$. We have
		\begin{align*}
			0& \ge \int_{\widetilde\Omega} |\nabla v_1|^{2}- \sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_j} v_1\,\partial_\nu u_+ \\
			& \ge \int_{\widetilde\Omega} |\nabla v_1|^{2}+ \gamma^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_j} (v_1^2 -v_1 u_- )\\
			& \ge \int_{\widetilde\Omega} |\nabla v_1|^{2} +  \gamma^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_j} (v_1^2 -v_1 v_2).
		\end{align*}
		We then multiply the second equation in \eqref{subrobin} by $k_j v_2$ and integrate by parts in $\mathcal{D}_j$, $j = 1,2$. We have
		\begin{align*}
			0& \ge \sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\mathcal{D}_j} k_j |\nabla v_2|^{2} + \sum_{j=1}^2 k_j \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_j} v_2\,\partial_\nu u_- \\
			& \ge \sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\mathcal{D}_j} k_j |\nabla v_2|^{2}+ \gamma^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_j} (v_2^2 -v_2 u_+) \\
			& \ge \sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\mathcal{D}_j} k_j |\nabla v_2|^{2} +  \gamma^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_j} (v_2^2 -v_1 v_2).
		\end{align*}
		Summing up the two inequalities above yields
		$$
		\int_{\widetilde\Omega} |\nabla v_1|^{2} + \sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\mathcal{D}_j} k_j |\nabla v_2|^{2} +  \gamma^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^2 \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_j} (v_1- v_2)^2 \le 0.
		$$
		Therefore,
		$$
		\nabla v_1 \equiv 0 ~\mbox{in}~\widetilde\Omega, \quad \nabla v_2 \equiv 0 ~\mbox{in}~\mathcal{D}_1 \cup \mathcal{D}_2, \quad v_1 \equiv v_2 ~\mbox{on}~ \partial \mathcal{D}_1 \cup \partial \mathcal{D}_2.
		$$
		Since $v_1 = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$, it follows that $v_1 \equiv 0$ in $\widetilde \Omega$, and hence $v_2 \equiv 0$ in $\mathcal{D}_1 \cup \mathcal{D}_2$. Therefore, \eqref{v_upper} is proved.

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $n\ge 2$, $\Omega$, $\mathcal{D}_1$, and $\mathcal{D}_2$ be Lipschitz domains in $ \mathbb{R}^n$, {and let $\varphi\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$. Then} $u$ is the minimizer of \eqref{minimizer} if and only if $u$ is a piecewise $ H^1$ solution to \eqref{robin}. Therefore, there exists a unique piecewise $ H^1$ solution $u$ to the equation \eqref{robin}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, by Lemma \ref{lem:maximum_principle}, we know that the equation \eqref{robin} has at most one solution. {For $\varphi\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, a trace lifting makes $\mathscr{A}$ nonempty. The boundary Poincar\'e and trace inequalities, together with the jump terms, 
        give coercivity on variations with zero outer trace. Weak lower semicontinuity yields a minimizer by the direct method, and strict positivity of the quadratic form on nonzero variations gives uniqueness.} Therefore, it suffices to show that the minimizer $u$ of \eqref{minimizer} satisfies \eqref{robin}.
		
		By a standard argument, one can see that the minimizer $u$ of \eqref{minimizer} is harmonic in $\widetilde\Omega$ and $\mathcal{D}_1 \cup \mathcal{D}_2$. It remains to show that $u$ satisfies the transmission conditions \eqref{robin}$_3$.
		
		We choose an arbitrary piecewise $H^1$ function $v$ such that $v = 0$ in $\mathcal{D}_1 \cup \mathcal{D}_2$ and on ${\partial (\Omega\setminus \overline \mathcal{D}_2)}$. Then the equation
		\begin{equation*}
			0 = \left.\frac{d}{dt} \right|_{t = 0}  I[u + t v]
		\end{equation*}
		{gives}
		$$
		0 = \int_{\widetilde\Omega} \nabla u_+ \cdot \nabla v_+ + \gamma^{-1} \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_1} (u_+ - u_-) v_+.
		$$
		Using the harmonicity of $u_+$ and integration by parts, we have
		$$
		0 = \int_{\partial \mathcal{D}_1} \big( \partial_\nu u_+ + \gamma^{-1}  (u_+ - u_-) \big) v_+,
		$$
		which implies 
		$$
		\partial_\nu u_+ =  -\gamma^{-1}(u_+-u_-)\qquad\mbox{on}~\partial \mathcal{D}_1.
		$$
		The rest of the transmission conditions follow similarly.

label: u_C0
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, \eqref{u_C0} simply follows from the maximum principle Lemma \ref{lem:maximum_principle}. For $i = 1, 2$, $u_-$ satisfies
		$$
		\begin{cases}
			\Delta u_- = 0&\mbox{in}~\mathcal{D}_i,\\ 
			\partial_\nu u_- = -(k_i\gamma)^{-1}(u_+-u_-)&\mbox{on}~\partial \mathcal{D}_i.
		\end{cases}
		$$
		By the $W^{1,p}$ estimate for the Neumann boundary problem (see \cite{DongLi21}*{Theorem 2.6}), we have
		$$
		\| u_- - (u_-)_{\mathcal{D}_i} \|_{W^{1,p}(\mathcal{D}_i)} \le  \frac{C}{k_i} \| u_+ - u_-\|_{ L^{p} (\partial \mathcal{D}_i)},
		$$
		which implies \eqref{u_holder_inside} by \eqref{u_C0} and Morrey's inequality. Recall that $u_+$ satisfies
		$$
		\begin{cases}
			\Delta u_+ = 0&\mbox{in}~\widetilde\Omega,\\ 
			\partial_\nu u_+ = {-}\gamma^{-1}(u_+-u_-)&\mbox{on}~\partial \mathcal{D}_1 \cup \partial \mathcal{D}_2,\\
			u_+ = \varphi &\mbox{on}~\partial \Omega.
		\end{cases}
		$$
		Away from the narrow gap region, one can apply a similar { local $W^{1,p}$ estimate} to see that
		$$
		[u_+]_{{C^{\beta}}(\widetilde\Omega \setminus \Omega_{R_0/4})} \le C \| \varphi\|_{C^\beta (\partial \Omega)}.
		$$
		Then one can apply the $C^{1,\beta}$ estimate for the Neumann boundary problem (see \cite{Lieberman87}*{Theorem 1.2}) to obtain
		$$
		\|u\|_{{C^{1,\beta}}(\widetilde\Omega \setminus \Omega_{R_0/2})} \le C \Big( [u_+]_{C^\beta(\widetilde\Omega \setminus \Omega_{R_0/4})} + {\|u_-\|_{C^\beta(\mathcal{D}_1)} + \|u_-\|_{C^\beta(\mathcal{D}_2)}} + \| \varphi\|_{C^{1,\beta} (\partial \Omega)} \Big),
		$$
		which implies \eqref{u_C1_outside}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lemma_reduction}, $\bar{v}$ satisfies \eqref{equation_v_bar} with $\mu=1$, $F$, $G_1$, and $G_2$ satisfying \eqref{FG_bound} with $\tilde{g}_i$ in place of $g_i$. In particular,
			$$G_2(y')=-\gamma^{-1}\sqrt{1+ |\nabla_{y'}h_1|^2} \tilde{g}_1(y') - \gamma^{-1}\sqrt{1+ |\nabla_{y'}h_2|^2} \tilde{g}_2(y').$$
			We then define
			$$
			\tilde{G}_2(y'):=
			\left\{
			\begin{aligned}
				&G_2(y'), &&\mbox{if } \gamma\neq 1,\\
				&-\gamma^{-1} ({g}_1(y')-g_1(0')+{g}_2(y')-g_2(0')), && \mbox{if } \gamma= 1,
			\end{aligned}
			\right.
			$$   
			and
			$$\tilde{G}_1(y'):=G_1(y')+G_2(y')-\tilde{G}_2(y').$$
			For the case when $\gamma\ne 1$, \eqref{FG_bound_b} follows from \eqref{FG_bound}, \eqref{tildeg}, \eqref{fg_0}, and \eqref{def:c_2}.
			For the case when $\gamma= 1$, by \eqref{u-_1+holder}, we have $\|\nabla g_i\|_{C^{\beta}}\le C/k_i$ and the estimate for $\tilde{G}_2$ follows. It remains to prove the estimate for $\tilde{G}_1$ when $\gamma=1$. Note that by the triangle inequality, \eqref{fg_0}, \eqref{def:c_2}, and \eqref{g1+g2}, 
			$$
			\begin{aligned}
				&|G_2(y')-\tilde{G}_2(y')|\le |G_2(y')+\gamma^{-1} (\tilde g_1(y')+\tilde{g}_2(y'))|
				\\&\qquad+|-\gamma^{-1} (\tilde g_1(y')+\tilde{g}_2(y'))+\gamma^{-1} ({g}_1(y')-g_1(0')+{g}_2(y')-g_2(0'))|\\
				&\le C |y'|^2.
			\end{aligned}
			$$
			Therefore, the estimate for ${\tilde G_1}$ follows from \eqref{FG_bound} and the last inequality. The lemma is proved.

title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, we assume that $\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\partial\Omega)}= 1$. Recall that $\mu = 1$. We will prove \eqref{grad_u_upperbound1_zero} and \eqref{grad_u_upperbound2_zero} with $\alpha_0$ given as in \eqref{alpha_new_zero}. As in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm_upperbound}, we perform the subtraction \eqref{subtr}, make the change of variables \eqref{x_to_y}, and let $v(y) = \tilde{u}(x)$, and let $\bar{v}$ be the vertical average defined as in \eqref{v_bar_def}. { Then by Lemma \ref{lemma_reduction_2}, $\bar{v}$ satisfies \eqref{equation_v_bar_2} with $F$, $\tilde{G}_1$, $\tilde{G}_2$ satisfying \eqref{FG_bound_b}. Since $|\nabla(a+b\cdot x)|=|b|\le C$, it suffices to prove the gradient estimates {\eqref{grad_u_upperbound1}, \eqref{grad_u_upperbound3}, and \eqref{grad_u_upperbound2}} for $\tilde{u}$. For simplicity of notation, we still denote $\tilde u$ by $u$, $\tilde{g}_i$ by $g_i$, and $\tilde{G}_i$ by $G_i$.} Note that
		the estimates
		\eqref{gi_c_beta}
		--
		\eqref{v-v_bar_2} still hold.
		On the other hand, $e^i$ in \eqref{a_ij_formula} can be bounded by $C|y'|^{2+\sigma}$. 
		
		Therefore, by Lemma \ref{lemma_reduction_2}, \eqref{grad_v_bar_start_2}, and \eqref{grad_n_v_bound_2}, $F,G_1,G_2$ satisfy
		\begin{equation}\label{F_G1_zero}
			\|F\|_{\varepsilon, \sigma, s_0, B_{R_0}} + \|G_1\|_{\varepsilon, \sigma-1, s_0, B_{R_0}}\le C,
		\end{equation}
		and 
		\begin{equation}\label{G2-1_zero}
			\|G_2\|_{\varepsilon, \sigma-1, s, B_{R_0}}\le C, \quad \mbox{when } \gamma\neq 1, \sigma\le 2s+\beta,
		\end{equation}
		
		\begin{equation}\label{G2-2_zero}
			\|G_2\|_{\varepsilon, \sigma-1, s, B_{R_0}}\le C, \quad \mbox{when } \gamma=1, \sigma\le 2s.
		\end{equation}
		Let $G:=G_1+G_2$.
		
		Next, we consider two separate cases: $\gamma\ne 1$ and $\gamma=1$.
		
		\textit{Case 1:} When $\gamma\ne 1$,
		by decreasing $\sigma$ if necessary, we may assume that $\sigma\le \beta$ (so that \eqref{G2-1_zero} is satisfied for any $s>0$), and $1+\sigma-2s_0=\sigma\ne\widehat\alpha_0$, where $\widehat{\alpha}_0 = \min\{\alpha_0, 1\}$.
		Then by \eqref{F_G1_zero} and \eqref{G2-1_zero} with $s=s_0$, the estimate \eqref{v_bar_L2_sphere_new} in Proposition \ref{prop_grad_v_bar_control} implies that 
		\begin{equation}\label{v_bar_decay_new}
			\nparallel\kern-.2em \bar{v} - \bar{v}(0) \Vert_{L^2(\partial B_{2\varepsilon^{1/2}})}\le C \varepsilon^{\tilde{\alpha}_0/2},
		\end{equation}
		where $\tilde{\alpha}_0 := \min\{\widehat\alpha_0 , 1+ \sigma - 2s_0 \}$.
		
		Then by \eqref{v_bar_decay_new}, \eqref{v-v_bar_2}, and the triangle inequality, we have
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}\label{v_L2_control_1_zero}
				\nparallel\kern-.2em u-(u)_{\Omega_{2\varepsilon^{1/2}}} \Vert_{L^2(\Omega_{2\varepsilon^{1/2}})} \le &\nparallel\kern-.2em u-\bar{v}(0) \Vert_{L^2(\Omega_{2\varepsilon^{1/2}})}  
				\\ \le &  C \nparallel\kern-.2em v-\bar v(0) \Vert_{L^2(Q_{2\varepsilon^{1/2} , \varepsilon})} \\
				\le& C( \nparallel\kern-.2em v-\bar{v} \Vert_{L^2(Q_{2\varepsilon^{1/2} , \varepsilon})} + \nparallel\kern-.2em \bar v-\bar{v}(0) \Vert_{L^2(Q_{2\varepsilon^{1/2} , \varepsilon})})\\
				\le& C \varepsilon^{\tilde\alpha_0/2}.
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		By \eqref{v_L2_control_1_zero}, \eqref{gi_c_beta}, and \eqref{gradient-1/2} with $g_1(0') = g_2(0') = 0$, we have
		$$
		\| \nabla u\|_{L^\infty (\Omega_{\varepsilon^{1/2}})} \le C\varepsilon^{\frac{\tilde\alpha_0-1}{2}}.
		$$
		Similarly, for any $R \in (\varepsilon^{1/2}, R_0/4)$,  the estimates \eqref{v_bar_L2_sphere_new} in Proposition \ref{prop_grad_v_bar_control} with $s=s_0$ and \eqref{v-v_bar} imply
		$$
		\nparallel\kern-.2em u-(u)_{\Omega_{4R}\setminus \Omega_{{R/4}}} \Vert_{L^2(\Omega_{4R}\setminus \Omega_{{R/4}})} \le C R^{\tilde\alpha_0}, 
		$$
		which implies, by \eqref{gradient-1/2} with $g_1(0') = g_2(0') = 0$ and \eqref{gi_c_beta},
		$$
		\| \nabla u\|_{L^\infty (\Omega_{{2R}}\setminus \Omega_{R/2})} \le CR^{\tilde\alpha_0-1}
		$$
		for any $R \in (\varepsilon^{1/2}, R_0/4)$. Therefore, we have improved the upper bound $|\nabla u(x)| \le C(\varepsilon + |x'|^2)^{-s_0}$ to $|\nabla u(x)| \le C(\varepsilon + |x'|^2)^{\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_0-1}{2}}$, where $\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_0-1}{2} = \min\left\{0,\frac{\alpha_0 - 1}{2}, -s_0 + \frac{\sigma}{2} \right\}$. If $-s_0 + \frac{\sigma}{2} <\min\left\{0, \frac{\alpha_0 - 1}{2}\right\}$, we take $s_1 = s_0 - \frac{\sigma}{2}$ and repeat the argument above. Note that the improved upper bound $|\nabla u(x)| \le C(\varepsilon + |x'|^2)^{-s_1}$ implies \eqref{F_G1_zero} with $s_1$ in place of $s_0$. Let $s_k=s_0-k\frac{\sigma}{2}$ for $k\in \mathbb{Z}_+$. We may decrease $\sigma$ if necessary so that $1+\sigma -2s_k\ne \widehat\alpha_0$ for any $k\in \mathbb{Z}_+$.
		After repeating the argument finitely many times, we obtain the estimate \eqref{grad_u_upperbound1_zero} or \eqref{grad_u_upperbound2_zero}.
		
		\textit{Case 2:} When $\gamma= 1$, {in contrast to Case 2 in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm_upperbound},} we know that $\widehat\alpha_0=\min\{\alpha_0,1\}=\alpha_0<1$. Let $s_k=s_0-k\frac{\sigma}{2}$ for $k\in \mathbb{Z}_+$. We may decrease $\sigma$ if necessary so that $\sigma< 1-\alpha_0$ and $1 -2s_k\ne \alpha_0$ for any $k\in \mathbb{Z}_+$. Note that we can repeat the argument as in Case 1 as long as $\sigma\le 2s_k$, so that \eqref{G2-2_zero} is satisfied. Let $j\in \mathbb{Z}_+$ such that $1 -2s_{j-1}< \alpha_0$ and $1 -2s_{j}> \alpha_0$. Then $\sigma<1-\alpha_0<2s_{j-1}\le 2s_{k}$ for $k\le j-1$ and one can repeat the argument as in Case 1, {using \eqref{G2-2_zero} instead of \eqref{G2-1_zero},} to obtain the upper bound $|\nabla u(x)| \le C(\varepsilon + |x'|^2)^\theta$,
		where $\theta:=\min\{\frac{\alpha_0-1}{2},-s_{j-1}+\frac{\sigma}{2}\}=\min\{\frac{\alpha_0-1}{2},-s_j\}=\frac{\alpha_0-1}{2}$.
		Therefore, the estimate {\eqref{grad_u_upperbound2_zero}} is proved.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v_+:=x_1$ in $\widetilde\Omega$ and $v_-=\frac{x_1}{1+k_i\gamma} \mbox{in }\mathcal{D}_i$, $i=1,2$. Then clearly 
		$$
		\Delta v_+=0 \quad \mbox{in } \widetilde{\Omega}, \quad \Delta v_-=0 \quad \mbox{in }\mathcal{D}_i, \quad i=1,2.
		$$
		Note that on $\partial\mathcal{D}_1\cup\partial\mathcal{D}_2$,
		$\partial_\nu x_1=-x_1$. Therefore, on $\partial\mathcal{D}_i$, $i=1,2$,
		\begin{equation*}                  
			\partial_\nu v_++\gamma^{-1}(v_+-v_-)=\big(\frac{k_i}{1+k_i\gamma}-1\big)x_1,\quad
			k_i\partial_\nu v_-+\gamma^{-1}(v_+-v_-)=0.
		\end{equation*} 
		Since $\gamma\ge 1$ and $k_1,k_2>0$, $$\frac{k_i}{1+k_i\gamma}-1 <0.$$
		Then we set $w=v-u$, namely $w_+=v_+-u_+$, $w_-=v_--u_-$. It suffices to show that 
		$w\le 0$ in $\Omega\cap\{x_1\ge 0\}$ and $w\ge 0$ in $\Omega\cap\{x_1\le 0\}$.   
		Clearly, $w$ satisfies 
		$$  
		\Delta w_+=0 \quad \mbox{in } \widetilde{\Omega}, \quad \Delta w_-=0 \quad \mbox{in }\mathcal{D}_i, \quad i=1,2
		$$
		and 
		on $\partial\mathcal{D}_i$, $i=1,2$,
		\begin{equation*}                  
			\partial_\nu w_++\gamma^{-1}(w_+-w_-)=\big(\frac{k_i}{1+k_i\gamma}-1\big)x_1,
		\end{equation*}
		\begin{equation*}                  
			k_i\partial_\nu w_-+\gamma^{-1}(w_+-w_-)=0.
		\end{equation*} 
		Therefore, $w$ is a subsolution
		of \eqref{robin} (as defined in Lemma \ref{lem:maximum_principle}
		in $\Omega\cap \{x_1>0\}$ and a supersolution in $\Omega\cap \{x_1<0\}$. We also know that $$w_+=0 \quad \mbox{on } \partial\Omega,$$
		and by symmetry, $u=0$ when $x_1=0$ and therefore $$w=0 \quad \mbox{on } \{x_1=0\}.$$
		Then by the maximum principle Lemma \ref{lem:maximum_principle} applied in  $\Omega\cap \{x_1>0\}$ and $\Omega\cap \{x_1<0\}$ respectively, we have
		$w\le 0$ in $\Omega\cap\{x_1\ge 0\}$ and $w\ge 0$ in $\Omega\cap\{x_1\le 0\}$. The proof is complete.
